<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This PKGBUILD is a standard binary-distribution package for Arch Linux. The `source` array points to the project's own GitHub releases (`github.com/poooi/poi`) for a `.deb` artifact, and a concrete `sha256sums` value is provided for verification. Sourcing the PKGBUILD only defines variables; there is no `pkgver()` function, no `eval`, no command substitution, and no network-exfiltration or code-execution logic in the top-level scope. The `package()` function uses standard tools (`bsdtar`, `chmod`, `mkdir`, `ln`) but is **not** executed under `--nobuild --noprepare`, so it is out of scope for this gate. Running the two requested commands will only fetch the declared upstream source and print metadata — no untrusted payload is downloaded or executed.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>Standard AUR binary package; no malicious code in gate-executable scope.</summary>
</security_assessment>

LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This PKGBUILD follows standard AUR packaging practices for a binary distribution package. It downloads a .deb release from the project's own GitHub repository (poooi/poi), verifies it with a proper SHA256 checksum (not SKIP), and packages it using bsdtar extraction (standard for .deb files).

The operations in package() are routine: extracting data.tar.xz, setting the chrome-sandbox binary to setuid (4755, which is standard for Electron/Chromium-based applications), creating a symlink in /usr/bin. The poi application is described as a "Scalable KanColle browser and tool," which is consistent with being an Electron-based application requiring the sandbox binary.

No malicious indicators are present: no obfuscated code, no unexpected network requests, no eval/base64/curl commands, no data exfiltration, and no backdoor installation. The source URL points to the declared upstream (github.com/poooi/poi), and the checksum is properly pinned.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>
Standard AUR binary PKGBUILD with no malicious indicators</security_assessment>

No network requests, downloads, obfuscation, or unexpected file operations are present. The use of /tmp for a temporary file is a common, low-risk practice consistent with ordinary packaging.
</details>
